title: Exploring the Applications of Generative AI in High School STEM Education
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether generative AI can improve educational outcomes in high school STEM classrooms, with a focus on physics. The central question is whether generative AI tools help or harm student learning, especially when students use them without explicit guidance on responsible and effective use. The author frames the study as a response to concerns about misinformation, overreliance, and academic dishonesty associated with general-purpose generative AI systems.

The study compares four conditions: a control group with no external resources, a search-engine condition, a generative AI condition using Bing AI (GPT-4 based), and a generative AI plus literacy program condition that included a slideshow on responsible and effective use. The intervention was implemented with AP Physics 1 and on-level physics students at Tomball Memorial High School in Texas. Students completed pre-tests, received a teacher lecture, studied for 20 minutes under their assigned condition, and then completed post-tests and a survey.

Results from the objective assessments suggested that generative AI without literacy support could be detrimental, with the GAI-only group performing worse than both the search engine group and the control group in AP Physics. In contrast, the generative AI literacy program improved performance relative to GAI alone, especially in AP Physics, though the treatment did not produce statistically significant gains over control overall in either section. Survey results showed no statistically significant differences in perceived understanding, engagement, or enjoyment, and the author concludes that generative AI may help only when paired with explicit literacy instruction, while short-term classroom use alone is insufficient to reliably improve outcomes.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental school-based study with pre/post testing and comparison groups, but it is not randomized, has uneven and sometimes small subgroup sizes, and relies on a single-school sample. The design is stronger than opinion/qualitative work, but it falls short of a well-controlled RCT/QED meeting higher-credibility standards.
impact_tier_rationale: The findings are mixed and the clearest positive effect is limited to a subgroup comparison in AP Physics rather than a broad, generalizable effect. The study reports no significant differences versus control in the main pre/post outcomes for either section, so the overall impact appears modest and unclear.

interventions.use_case: High school physics students used Bing AI (GPT-4-based) as a generative AI study aid for concept review and problem support during a 20-minute out-of-class study period. The paper also tested the same tool with and without a brief generative AI literacy slideshow explaining responsible and effective use.
Search engine-based study support (Google) used as a non-generative digital reference tool for physics topic review, serving as a comparison condition against generative AI.

finding.finding_summary: The quasi-experimental study (n=171 total; AP Physics n=91, on-level physics n=80) found that generative AI without literacy support underperformed compared with control and search-engine conditions in AP Physics, with mean pre/post score differences of -0.857 for GAI versus 0.484 for SE and -0.346 for control. In contrast, the GAI + literacy program condition improved relative to GAI (0.500 vs -0.857), and the AP Physics ANOVA was significant (p=0.011), but on-level physics showed no significant differences (p=0.619).
finding.measure: Pre-test to post-test score difference on physics assessments (AP Physics momentum/impulse; on-level physics electricity/circuits)
finding.std_deviation: AP Physics SDs: control 1.355, SE 1.387, GAI 1.791, GAI-LP 1.225; on-level SDs: control 1.700, SE 2.250, GAI 2.199, GAI-LP 1.569

finding.finding_summary: Survey results suggested only small, non-significant differences in understanding, engagement, and enjoyment across groups, with the GAI group reporting slightly higher engagement but overlapping confidence intervals and a MANOVA that was not significant (p=0.115). The paper interprets generative AI as potentially increasing engagement, but the observed effect in this short intervention was weak and not statistically reliable.
finding.measure: Post-survey ratings of understanding, confidence, engagement, and enjoyment
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CIs overlapped across groups; MANOVA p=0.115

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI literacy may improve responsible use, ethical awareness, and self-confidence in using generative AI, but the direct survey evidence was weak: most GAI-LP respondents rated the literacy program as having no impact (mode=3 on a 1-5 scale). Still, the GAI-LP condition showed better academic performance than GAI alone in AP Physics, suggesting some support for improved metacognitive use even though perceived benefit was low.
finding.measure: Post-survey perception of literacy-program impact; inferred responsible/effective AI-use readiness

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests schools should not ban generative AI outright and should instead implement AI literacy programs and clearer classroom policies. This is based on the observed pattern that GAI without guidance could be detrimental, while GAI with literacy training improved AP Physics outcomes relative to GAI alone.
finding.measure: Policy implications drawn from experimental comparison of treatment conditions
